LESSON 13 OF 106·Networking Fundamentals

HTTP/HTTPS and the Request–Response Cycle

How an HTTP request and response are built, what TLS changes about them, and why status codes, headers and cookies carry real security meaning.

Beginner15 min
Why this matters

HTTP is a request-response protocol: a client asks for a resource, a server answers with a status and content. Almost everything you do in a browser is this cycle, which is why most web attacks target it.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • A request carries a method such as GET or POST, a path, headers, and optionally a body.
  • The response carries a status code, headers, and a body, and the two are independent of each other.
  • HTTP is stateless by design, so state lives in cookies, tokens or URLs, and each of those becomes a security decision.
  • HTTPS is HTTP carried inside TLS, which encrypts the path, authenticates the server by name, and protects integrity.
  • TLS negotiates a modern version and cipher suite before any application data is sent, and a failure there stops the request before it leaves.

The background

  • HTTP began as a simple document-retrieval protocol and grew method by method into a general request-response model.
  • Cookies were added to carry state, and remain the source of many session-management weaknesses.
  • The move to HTTPS across major sites was driven by both security and browser pressure, and mixed-content blocking finished the job.
  • Modern versions add multiplexing and better caching, but the request-response shape has stayed constant.

Real-world examples

  • A page loaded over HTTPS that requests an image over HTTP is still downgradeable, which is why mixed content is blocked.
  • A redirect from HTTPS to HTTP exposes cookies that were not marked secure, which is how session theft usually starts.
  • A cached response served to the wrong user is a header problem, not a cryptography problem.

What to look for

  • Check that the first request on any page is already HTTPS, not upgraded after loading content.
  • Look for cookies without the secure flag, especially session identifiers.
  • Notice whether redirects cross between schemes or hosts in a way that changes what the browser trusts.
  • Check cache-control on anything sensitive, since a cached page can be served to a different person.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Redirect to HTTPS before serving any content, and serve HSTS so browsers refuse to fall back.
  • Mark session cookies secure, HttpOnly and SameSite.
  • Set explicit cache-control on authenticated and personal responses.
  • Keep certificate renewal automated, because an expired certificate trains users to click through warnings.
